title: Malik ibn Anas
hook: the imam of Medina, who would not ride in the Prophet's city out of respect (reported)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Hanifa and the judge's seat he would not take, and your line: he refused the post. Did you need your short, kind no? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

Fine horses stand tied outside a scholar's door in Medina. Gifts, he explains to a visiting student. The student asks the natural question: then why not ride one? The answer, as his biographers tell it, is that he would be ashamed before Allah to tread with a hoof on ground where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lies buried. So in the city of the Prophet, he walked. The student in that story is said to be a young al-Shafi'i, whom we'll meet properly soon. The man on foot founded the next school on this path. Today: Malik ibn Anas.
screen: `HORSES AT THE DOOR.` → `WHY NOT RIDE ONE?` → `IN THE PROPHET'S CITY, HE WALKED.`

segments.voice: Begin with place. Abu Hanifa was a man of Kufa, a busy city of merchants and debates. Malik was a man of Medina, the city where the Prophet lived, prayed, taught and was buried. He was born there, taught there, and, the reports say, rarely left except for pilgrimage. That's why the index calls him the imam of Medina. Next, the respect. The horse story isn't the only one. His biographers say that before he taught hadith he would wash, put on good clothes and perfume, and sit with dignity, because the words were the Prophet's. A story people tell has a scorpion stinging him again and again during a lesson, and Malik not stopping until the hadith was finished. Whether every detail is exact, the picture is consistent: a man who treated the Prophet's words as you'd treat a guest of honor. Then, his honesty. A traveler is said to have come a long way with a list of questions, and Malik answered question after question with two words: la adri, I don't know. The man protested that he'd come so far. Malik's reply, in the report, is to tell people that Malik doesn't know. For a jurist, saying I don't know was a form of respect too. Last, a line attributed to him while pointing at the Prophet's grave: everyone's word can be taken or left, except the one in this grave. Some reports give versions of it to others. Either way, it fits the man: careful with the Prophet's city, careful with his words, and careful with his own.
screen: `THE IMAM OF MEDINA.` · `WASHED AND PERFUMED TO TEACH HADITH.` · `LA ADRI: I DON'T KNOW.` · `EVERYONE'S WORD, EXCEPT ONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: walk somewhere respectfully. If you can stand and walk a few steps, do it now, slowly, inside your room. If you can't, choose a place in your memory that deserves care: a grave you've visited, a house of worship, your grandmother's kitchen. Walk into it in your mind. Notice your feet, your pace, your voice getting lower. Notice what you'd touch and what you wouldn't. Then stop where you are and stand still for a moment. If you pray, you can greet that place with a greeting your tradition uses. The bell holds the time.
Malik ibn Anas. The imam of Medina, founder of the Maliki school, remembered for his respect for the Prophet's city and words, and for saying I don't know. Today's word.
Your line: the imam of medina. Today, when someone asks you something you don't actually know, try saying so plainly, the way Malik did. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Maliki Muslims remember Imam Malik as the scholar of Medina who taught hadith with great reverence and was willing to say 'I don't know'; his school is followed in North and West Africa.
